zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical review aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0; supplied page subset). Used for lexical cross-checks after reading the BnF scan, not as authority for this copy's spelling, typography, or placement. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Gokugetsu is the final lunar month, identified as shiwasu. The printed final t in Gocuguet is retained, while Qiuamatta tçuqi supplies the Japanese explanation.
Duodecima lũa specifies the twelfth moon or lunar month. The nasal abbreviation remains unexpanded.
This goku-i means the highest rank or dignity, explained by kiwamatta kurai. The internal hyphen separates the vowels and is not a physical line-break mark.
Dade completes dignidade. The divided Portuguese word has no added hyphen on the preceding row.
This separate goku-i is the innermost meaning or essence. The scan supports cocoro, correcting OCR cotoro; the Portuguese explanation continues across the next row.

runs.text: ou amago dalgũa ley, ſciencia, arte, &c.

lines.note: The essence may be that of a law, science, or art. Amago supplies the idea of the core, and the historical spellings and tilde in dalgũa are retained.

runs.text: Gocujǒ. Qiuamaru vye. i, Iǒjǒno coto.

lines.note: Gokujo means the very highest, explained by kiwamaru ue and jojo. The initial I in Iǒjǒno has consonantal value here and is not changed to modern J.
The Portuguese gives something supreme or excellent. Item introduces a second application of the same word.

runs.text: Hũa laya de Cha a milhor que ha.

lines.note: The second application is the finest available kind of tea. Cha occurs inside a Portuguese explanation and is marked separately for possible whole-word typeface review.
Gokumi denotes excellent flavour, with kiwamatta ajiwai providing the Japanese analysis. The Portuguese adjective modifies the nouns on the next row.
Goſto and ſabor complete the taste definition. Their pairing confirms that the entry concerns flavour rather than a general preference.

runs.text: Lugar onde ſe prègão, ou poem as

lines.note: Gokumon is the place where the heads of executed people are nailed up or displayed. The historical prègão is retained in the Portuguese relative clause.
The displayed objects are the executed people's heads. The example kubi wo goku- begins a phrase about exposing a head at that place.
Monni completes gokumon ni, and kakuru supplies the act of placing or hanging. The Portuguese translation describes putting up the head of someone executed.
The execution and exposure are public. This row completes the example's translation rather than starting another judicial entry.
Gokunetsu is extreme heat, explained by kiwamatta atsusa. The headword's final checked t is preserved rather than expanded.
Quentura and calma both describe heat in this context. Calma should not be read as the modern English notion of tranquillity.
Gokuraku is a paradise of delights. The scan supports G and Tanoximiuo, 'bringing enjoyment to its utmost', rather than OCR C and Tanoxiniuo.
So completes Paraiſo. The phrase identifies a paradise of delights, finishing the gokuraku definition.

Gokuryo denotes the lord's own revenues or domain. The gloss makes kimi no onchigyo the likely intended explanation, but the scan's worn Qimiro is retained as the chosen literal reading rather than silently changing r to n.

runs.text: ou terras que o ſenhor tem aplicadas aſi ſem

lines.note: The lord keeps these revenues or lands assigned to himself. The tightly printed aſi is preserved, and the negative qualification continues below.
The lands are not distributed among the lord's retainers. Criados, not OCR criadoa, completes the contrast with the lord's personal domain.
This gokuro means extreme old age, explained by kiwamatta oi. The small stop after Qiuamatta is retained despite separating the adjective from its noun.
The example uses the humble verb tsukamatsutta to say that the speaker has reached great old age. The translation begins 'I am' and continues below.
Muito velho completes the statement 'I am very old'. It belongs to the age entry, not the following respectful word for trouble.
This second gokuro denotes trouble or labour spoken of respectfully. Its honorific qualification continues on the next row.

Vt introduces a respectful request to undertake the trouble. The damaged second t in atte is read from its faint stem and the Japanese construction; the OCR paragraph-sign-plus-t is an erroneous rendering of italic Vt.

runs.text: çouos q̃ ainda q̃ ſeja trabalho façais iſto, &c.

lines.note: Pe- plus çouos forms the request 'I ask you': please do this even though it involves trouble. Both q̃ abbreviations remain unexpanded.
Gokusoku is marked as Buddhist terminology and described as the chief point of meditation. Bup. is a roman domain label, distinct from the italic Portuguese definition.
The meditation is that of the Ienxus, referring to the Zen school. The Japanese school-name is embedded in the Portuguese sentence; the printed nasal abbreviation in taçoẽs is retained.

Gokusotsu denotes hell's executioners or demons. Acqi is supported by its visible q-descender, correcting OCR acei; the damaged Gigocuro is retained with r, although the intended explanation is evidently jigoku no akki.
Ferno completes inferno, followed by 'or devils'. This confirms the infernal-agent sense of the preceding Japanese entry.
Gokusui means profound sleep, explained by kiwamatta nemuri. The Portuguese adjective continues into the noun below.
Sono completes 'deep sleep'. The closing S. is a roman written-usage label and is separated from the italic gloss.
Gokutsubushi is someone useful for nothing beyond eating. The scan and supplied headword index both support initial G, rather than modernizing the word to a form beginning K or retaining OCR C.
The person is fit for nothing except eating. This completes the dismissive definition without adding a register label absent from the print.
The example gokushinna hito describes a person whose heart is peaceful. Its Portuguese noun phrase continues on the next row.

runs.text: de grande paz, & ſoſego do coração. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The person's heart has great peace and repose. Item then signals another sense of the same headword.
Muito aprimorado adds the sense 'highly refined' or 'perfected'. The short row remains a distinct physical continuation.
Gokusho is the place of confinement, explained by hitoya no tokoro. Tronco is used here in the prison or detention sense, not merely as a tree trunk.
Lugar da priſão completes the definition as the place of imprisonment. This confirms the confinement sense of Tronco above.
Gokusho, alternatively gokushona, describes something extremely small or scanty. The circumflexes distinguish this entry's printed form from the unmarked prison word.
Na completes pequena, followed by pouca. The definition combines small size with small amount.
Gokuyaku is obligatory service performed by someone. The person to whom it is owed is specified on the next row.
The service is rendered to the lord who commands it. The relative clause completes the preceding social-duty definition.
Gokuzai is a consummate or extreme offence, explained by kiwamatta tsumi. The scan supports Qiuamatta and con-, not OCR Qiuanatta and cen-.
Sumado completes conſumado. The next column's Gocuzainin develops the related word for a person steeped in such wrongdoing.
Goku-zainin is a person extreme in wrongdoing, explained by tsumi ni kiwamatta hito. Ho continues as Homem below without an added line-end hyphen.
Mem completes Homem: a person steeped in sins and wickedness. The scan supports peccados, correcting OCR peceados.

Godai is the future age, also named Côtai. Enlarged second-pass inspection shows faint upward-pointing accent strokes over o, so Côtai is chosen instead of OCR Cǒtai; the worn apex remains a nonblocking graphic uncertainty. The Portuguese continues with futura below.
The example godai no tameshi ni suru concerns making an example for future generations. Dei continues into the Portuguese verb on the next row, with no supplied hyphen.

runs.text: xar exemplo, ou eſcarmento pera o futuro.

lines.note: Xar completes deixar: leaving an example or warning for the future. Futuro, not OCR fuluro, agrees with the time-reference throughout this entry.
Godo is a violent robber, explained as tsuyoi nusubito. Both printed carons are retained, and the Portuguese adds a forceful characterization below.
Esfola caras is an expressive description of the violent robber. The spaced words are preserved rather than replaced with a modern compound.
This godo is Buddhist and concerns the way of attaining understanding. The d in Godǒ corrects OCR c; me- begins the Portuguese meditar below.

runs.text: ditar, & entender as couſas do Buppô.

lines.note: The definition is meditation and understanding matters of Buddhism. The scan shows Buppô with two p letters and a circumflex, not OCR Bupò; it is embedded in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Hũa laya de Sacazzuqui de barro

lines.note: Godoiri names a kind of earthenware drinking cup. Sacazzuqui is Japanese vocabulary within the Portuguese explanation, and its size is specified below.
Grande makes this a large earthenware cup. The short row belongs to the preceding vessel entry.
Gohatsu refers to the tips of hairs. The initial Portuguese P is visible in Pontinhas, correcting OCR Fontinhas, while ca- continues below.
Bellos completes cabellos: the hairs of the head. This confirms the meaning of camigue no saki in the Japanese explanation.
Gohei consists of cut papers suspended from a small stick. The initial G corrects OCR C, and the Portuguese sentence continues across the next two rows.

runs.text: hum paoſinho de que vſão os gentios nas cere-

lines.note: The small stick is used by the people the compilers call gentios in ceremonies. The visible i restores gentios; paoſinho is retained without modernizing its consonant spelling.
The ceremonies take place before the kami. Cami is a Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese sentence.
Gohen, explained by kisho, is a respectful form of address. Voßa mercè gives the corresponding Portuguese courtesy expression, with its historical accent retained.
Goho, explained by onkata, has the same respectful-address sense. The scan supports Gofǒ rather than OCR Cufǒ; Idem refers to the preceding courtesy gloss.
Gofun is here explained broadly as enogu, coloured pigments or paints. The gloss does not justify narrowing it to one modern pigment composition.
Pintar completes 'coloured paints for painting'. The damaged first vowel and following n support pintar rather than OCR pentar.
Goga is a sea or river inlet. Enſeada corrects the OCR's extra c; the tight ourio is retained as printed spacing rather than automatically separated.
Goji concerns protection of the Buddhist teaching. The headword is Gogi, not OCR Ciogi, and pro continues into the next row's Portuguese noun without an added hyphen.

runs.text: teição do Cami ſobre as couſas do

lines.note: The gloss attributes guardianship over Buddhist matters to the kami. Buppô is visibly roman here, unlike the surrounding italic Portuguese; the separate Bup. is a domain label, not part of the name.
Gojin is the army's rear guard. Enlargement resolves the Japanese explanation as Vxirogin, ushirojin, rather than OCR Vxuogin, and confirms initial G in the headword.
This second gojin is Buddhist and is explained as five defilements. The Portuguese begins a definition in terms of sensory objects.

runs.text: obiectos dos ſentidos que custumão macular o

lines.note: The five objects of the senses are said to stain or defile a person. This is the dictionary's moral-religious explanation, not a modern scientific classification.
Homem completes the object of macular: the person is defiled. The one-word continuation is retained as a physical body row.
Gojo is an order from a noble person. The concise gloss distinguishes it from the neighbouring Buddhist entries.
Gojoku is explained by five forms of turbidity or impurity. The Portuguese describes five stains, with an alternative explanation below.
The alternative gloss is the ugliness or deformity of sins. Fealdades is one printed word, correcting the OCR's fealda des.
Gogo here means moving or acting, explained by ugoki hataraku. The scan supports Gǒgo rather than the OCR fragment Crôgo.
The positive and negative itaſu and itaſanu give movement and inability to move. Latin l separates alternatives, and the Portuguese continues below.

runs.text: não ſe poder mouer, nem andar.

lines.note: The negative gloss is being unable to move or walk. It completes the paired examples rather than defining a new word.
Unmarked Gogo means afterwards or in the future, with nochi as its Japanese explanation. The example is on the next row.

The example extends the time-reference to the final ages. The damaged t of matdai is compatible with the checked-coda spelling, and vltimos retains the historical initial v; the OCR paragraph sign is absent from the scan.
Pos completes tempos, followed by 'the last age'. This finishes the example about the remotest future.
This gogo means after midday. The closing S. is a roman written-usage label, separate from the italic Portuguese gloss.
Gogo, explained by miushiro, denotes the rear of the room in which the ruler sits. Zaxiqui is the Japanese room-name embedded in the gloss; the adjoining on- begins Portuguese onde.
De completes onde: the room is where the king is. The short continuation belongs to the spatial, not the afternoon, entry.
Gogo here is strength or rough forcefulness. The headword's faint second caron is retained; tçuyoxi, with a damaged rounded o, corrects OCR tçuyexi and supplies the adjective paired with tçuyoqu.
Hito completes the example of a strong, fierce, or harsh person. The Portuguese alternatives explain its forceful rather than merely energetic sense.

runs.text: Goguen. Itçutçuno manaco. i, Guen, ni,

lines.note: The entry labels five eyes through manaco but then lists guen and ni, continuing with other faculties below. That tension in the dictionary's explanation is preserved rather than harmonized.
Bi, jet, and xin complete the list, rendered collectively as five senses. Jet retains the checked final t; the list is not silently rewritten to match the preceding 'five eyes' wording.
Gogi means force or violence, explained by tsuyoi koto. The gloss is the abstract notion illustrated on the next row.
Gogi ni oyobu means going so far as to employ force. The Portuguese 'come to use force' confirms the construction without changing the printed voyobu spelling.
Gogyaku introduces five grave offences. The damaged o in the headword is read with the surviving outline and the continuation on f245; the visible gap in ſacay ima is retained rather than normalized.

runs.text: cados grauiſsimos de matar Fotoque. Vt,

lines.note: The list begins with killing a Buddha, using Fotoque within the Portuguese gloss. The scan supports grauiſsimos with a long and a short s, not OCR grauiſimnos. Fo- starts the Japanese example continued on f245; the bottom toqeuo repeats that continuation as a catchword.
Roman catchword repeating the opening fragment on f0245. The final body Fo- and that opening toqeuo belong to the running example; this repetition remains separate furniture.
